hints: Think about what type of compound phenol is. It has an $\text{OH}$ group attached to a ring, so it behaves as a weak acid and will react with bases and with reactive metals.
Recall the two general routes to a phenoxide salt: a metal can displace the phenolic $\text{H}$, while a metal hydroxide or oxide will neutralise the acid.
For each route, work out what is left over after $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$ pairs with $\text{K}^+$. A metal gives a gas, a hydroxide or oxide gives a neutral liquid.
walkthrough:
See phenol as a weak acid**
Picture $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ losing its $\text{OH}$ proton to leave $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$. Any potassium base will take that $\text{H}^+$ and leave $\text{K}^+$ to pair with the phenoxide ion. That is why phenol, unlike benzene, forms a salt.

First route with the metal**
Potassium metal is a strong reducing agent. It gives an electron to $\text{H}^+$ from two phenol molecules: $$2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2\text{K} \rightarrow 2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-\text{K}^+ + \text{H}_2$$ So substance is $\text{K}$ and the second product is hydrogen gas, $\text{H}_2$.

Second different route with a base**
A completely different substance is the alkali $\text{KOH}$ (accept $\text{K}_2\text{O}$ as alternative). This is simple neutralisation: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{KOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-\text{K}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ So substance is $\text{KOH}$ and the second product is water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Final answer: substance 1: $\text{K}$ / potassium, second product: $\text{H}_2$ / hydrogen
substance 2: $\text{KOH}$ / potassium hydroxide (or $\text{K}_2\text{O}$ / potassium oxide), second product: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ / water
$2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2\text{K} \rightarrow 2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-\text{K}^+ + \text{H}_2$; $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{KOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-\text{K}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: Look for the linking group that joins the two aromatic parts in Sudan I and contains nitrogen. This extended conjugated system absorbs visible light.
walkthrough:
Spot the colour causing group**
Sudan I is orange because it has a long conjugated system that absorbs visible light. The key part is the $\text{N}=\text{N}$ azo linkage between the two ring systems. Circling that double bond identifies the chromophore that makes it a dye.
Final answer: Circle the $\text{N}=\text{N}$ / azo bond linking the naphthol ring to the phenyl ring.

hints: Start from phenylamine, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$. To make an azo dye you must first convert the $\text{NH}_2$ group into a diazonium group. Recall which small inorganic acid is used for this.
Think about the temperature needed to keep the diazonium ion, $[\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+]$, stable and why ice cooling below $10\,^\circ\text{C}$ is essential.
Consider how the diazonium ion then joins to 2-naphthol. Recall the alkaline conditions that activate the naphthol ring for coupling.
walkthrough:
Make the diazonium ion first**
Dissolve phenylamine in cold dilute $\text{HCl}$ and add nitrous acid, $\text{HNO}_2$, keeping the mixture at or below $10\,^\circ\text{C}$ with ice. The $\text{NH}_2$ group is diazotised: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + \text{HNO}_2 + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow [\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+] + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Cold conditions are vital because the diazonium ion decomposes to give nitrogen gas if warmed.

Couple with activated 2-naphthol**
Dissolve 2-naphthol in aqueous $\text{NaOH}$. In alkali it exists as the naphthoxide ion, which is much more reactive toward electrophiles. Add the cold diazonium solution to this alkaline solution.

Form the azo link**
The diazonium ion acts as an electrophile and attacks the activated naphthol ring, forming the $\text{N}=\text{N}$ bridge. That coupling step produces the orange Sudan I dye.

Final answer: React phenylamine with $\text{HNO}_2$ (made from $\text{NaNO}_2$ + $\text{HCl}$) at $T \le 10\,^\circ\text{C}$ to form benzenediazonium ion, $[\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+]$. Then add 2-naphthol dissolved in aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ / alkali for azo coupling to give Sudan I.

hints: Recall that benzene needs very powerful nitrating conditions to make nitrobenzene. Think about what acids and temperature that uses.
Phenol nitrates much more easily, so imagine using only one dilute acid at room temperature with no catalyst. Explain why milder conditions prove higher reactivity.
walkthrough:
State the mild conditions**
Phenol needs only dilute aqueous nitric acid, $\text{HNO}_3(\text{aq})$, at room temperature to give 2-nitrophenol. No sulfuric acid catalyst and no heating are needed.

Compare with benzene to prove reactivity**
Benzene will not react with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$. It needs a nitrating mixture of concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ and concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ heated to about $50\,^\circ\text{C}$ to generate enough $\text{NO}_2^+$. Because phenol achieves nitration with far less forcing conditions, its ring must be more electron rich and more reactive toward electrophiles.

Final answer: conditions: dilute / aqueous $\text{HNO}_3$ at room temperature.
explanation: benzene requires concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ + concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and heating (about $50\,^\circ\text{C}$); phenol reacts under much milder conditions without $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ or heating, so phenol is more reactive.

hints: Focus on the oxygen atom of the $\text{OH}$ group. It has non-bonding electrons in a p-orbital that can overlap with the pi system of the ring.
walkthrough:
See the OH group donating electrons**
The oxygen in $\text{OH}$ has a lone pair in a p-orbital that sits alongside the ring pi system. That pair delocalises into the ring, pushing extra electron density into it. A more electron rich ring attracts the electrophile $\text{NO}_2^+$ more strongly, so electrophilic substitution is faster than in benzene.
Final answer: The lone pair / p-orbital on the oxygen of the $\text{OH}$ group delocalises / donates into the benzene ring, increasing electron density.

hints: Start the mechanism as for benzene: the pi electrons of the ring attack the electrophile. Think about where the first curly arrow starts and ends.

Draw the resulting intermediate with the $\text{OH}$ still attached, the new $\text{NO}_2$ and the $\text{H}$ on the same tetrahedral carbon, and the positive charge spread around the rest of the ring.
To restore aromaticity, a $\text{C-H}$ bond at that carbon must break. Think about where that pair of electrons goes.
walkthrough:
Attack of the ring on the electrophile**
Draw a curly arrow starting in the centre of the phenol ring pi system and pointing to the $\text{N}$ atom of $^+\text{NO}_2$. The pair of pi electrons forms a new $\text{C-N}$ bond at the 2-position. This is electrophilic attack.

Draw the stabilised intermediate**
The carbon that is attacked becomes $\text{sp}^3$ and carries three groups: the original $\text{H}$, the new $\text{NO}_2$, with the $\text{OH}$ on the adjacent carbon. The ring loses aromaticity and carries a positive charge delocalised over the remaining five carbons. Show the + in the ring and the tetrahedral carbon clearly.

Restore the aromatic ring**
Draw a second curly arrow starting from the $\text{C-H}$ bond on that tetrahedral carbon and going back into the ring. The $\text{C-H}$ bond breaks, $\text{H}^+$ leaves, and the electron pair reforms the pi system to give 2-nitrophenol.

Final answer: Curly arrow from phenol ring pi bond to $\text{N}$ of $^+\text{NO}_2$; intermediate is arenium ion with $\text{OH}$, $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{H}$ on saturated $\text{C}$ (2-position) and + charge delocalised in ring; curly arrow from $\text{C-H}$ bond into ring to reform aromatic product.

hints: The $\text{OH}$ group directs incoming electrophiles to the positions ortho and para to itself. You already have the 2-isomer, so think of the other activated position.
walkthrough:
Name the para isomer**
The $\text{OH}$ group is 2,4-directing. Nitration at the 2-position gives 2-nitrophenol, and attack at the equivalent para position gives the other major product, 4-nitrophenol.
